# Example output: Claude's response using voice.md

*This was generated by pasting `voice.md` as the opening message, then
providing the bullet points in `input.md`. It demonstrates the
define-then-translate pattern, the unexpected comparison as a reference
class for an abstract number, zoom out before zooming in, and consequences
facing outward toward the customer.*

---

Net Interest Margin is the spread between what the bank earns on its loans
and investments and what it pays depositors for the privilege of using their
money, expressed as a percentage of earning assets. In plain terms: it is
the bank's operating margin, and at a community bank it is almost the entire
business model. Unlike a software company that can grow revenue by shipping
a new feature, a community bank grows NIM by making better decisions about
who to lend to, at what rate, funded by deposits it attracts at the lowest
defensible cost. Every product you will ever work on here touches this number
somewhere. A new checking account that attracts sticky, low-cost deposits
expands it. A clunky loan application that loses borrowers to the credit
union down the street compresses it. NIM at most community banks sits
somewhere between 3% and 4%, which sounds like a rounding error until you
remember that the entire institution's ability to make payroll, absorb loan
losses, and reinvest in the community runs through that narrow corridor.

---

## What to notice in this output

| Voice rule | How it shows up |
|---|---|
| Define-then-translate | "Net Interest Margin is [precise definition]. In plain terms: [human version]." |
| Unexpected comparison | Software company analogy gives a tech PM an immediate reference class |
| Inline data with reference class | 3-4% "sounds like a rounding error" — the number lands because of what follows it |
| Consequences face outward | "loses borrowers to the credit union down the street" names the customer situation, not the internal metric |
| Humanity first | The credit union competitor makes it specific; a person is losing a real thing |
| No hedging | Every sentence states a fact. Nothing is "potentially" or "may" |
| Brevity | One paragraph. No wind-up. No summary sentence at the end. |
